opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's one of the most elegant ideas in all of machine learning, and it's a little underappreciated because people focus on the "beat Lee Sedol" headline.

The setup is this: you have a policy network that, given a board position, outputs a distribution over moves. On its own, that network is decent but imperfect. Then you run Monte Carlo Tree Search on top of it. The search uses the policy as a prior and the value network to evaluate leaf positions, and after a few hundred or thousand simulations you get a visit-count distribution over moves at the root. That distribution is strictly better than what the raw policy gave you, because it has "thought ahead."

The beautiful part is that you then train the policy network to match the search distribution. You're distilling the result of expensive deliberation back into a single forward pass. And now that the policy is better, the next round of search starts from a better prior, so the search gets better too. It's a bootstrapping loop where search improves the network and the network improves the search, and it doesn't need human data at all, which is what AlphaGo Zero showed.

What I love about it is that it's a very clean answer to a deep question: where does the improvement signal come from if you don't have a teacher? Here the teacher is just the model plus more compute at inference time. You spend test-time compute to generate a better target, then amortize it into the weights. It's System 2 thinking being compiled into System 1 intuition, over and over.

And I think that's exactly why it feels so relevant right now. With language models we're asking the same question: can we use reasoning, sampling, verification, or search at inference time to produce answers better than the model's default, and then train on those to lift the base model? Go made it work cleanly because you have a perfect simulator and an unambiguous win/loss signal. The open problem is how much of that recipe transfers to messier domains like code, math, robotics, or open-ended conversation, where your "search" and your "value function" are much noisier. But the core shape of the idea, improve the target with compute and then distill, is something I keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: The response says MCTS produces a root visit-count distribution and that the policy is trained to match that distribution, distinguishing it from a single selected action.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose retraining on MCTS-selected actions as a test of the importance of soft targets.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing that gets me about AlphaGo, and really AlphaZero which is the cleaner version of the idea, is that it's a bootstrapping loop where search is the teacher and the network is the student, and the student slowly becomes as good as the teacher so that the teacher can get even better.

Here's what I mean. You have a policy network that, given a board, spits out a distribution over moves. On its own it's okay, it's "intuition." Then you run Monte Carlo tree search on top of it. The search uses the policy as a prior to decide which branches are worth exploring, and after a few hundred or a few thousand simulations it produces a visit-count distribution over moves at the root. That distribution is strictly better than the raw policy, because it's had the benefit of actually looking ahead and seeing which moves hold up.

And the beautiful part is what they do with that. They don't just play the best move and move on. They take that improved distribution and use it as the target for the policy network. Cross-entropy, basically: make the one-shot intuition look like what the search would have said. So the network is being trained to amortize search. You're compressing an expensive, slow, deliberate computation into a fast forward pass.

Then the next time you search, you're starting from a stronger prior, so the search is more efficient and finds better moves, so the targets get better, so the network gets better. It's a closed loop where every iteration raises the ceiling on the next one. There's no human data in it. The only ground truth coming from outside is "did you win," and everything else is the system teaching itself.

I think the reason I keep coming back to it is that it feels like a general recipe, not a Go trick. You have "system one" and "system two," fast and slow, and the trick is to make system two's outputs supervise system one. You see the same shape in a lot of places now: expert iteration, the way people distill chain-of-thought into models, policy improvement in RL generally. Policy iteration in the classical sense is the same idea in disguise, actually. Evaluate, improve, make the policy greedy with respect to the improved estimate, repeat. AlphaGo just made it concrete with a neural network in the loop, and showed it scales to something that humans had assumed required this almost mystical pattern recognition.

The other thing that's elegant is how little is being asked of the network at any given step. It doesn't have to make a giant leap. It just has to get a little bit closer to what search already found. Each gradient step is small and well-posed, but the compounding over millions of games is enormous. That's a very different flavor from "collect a bunch of expert games and hope you generalize." It's self-improvement with a built-in mechanism for generating its own supervision, and that mechanism is just search.

r001.rationale: The response says the policy network is trained on the improved MCTS visit-count distribution, rather than simply playing the best move.

r002.rationale: It contrasts training on the distribution with playing the best move, but does not propose retraining on MCTS-selected actions to test the importance of soft targets.

astra-6.text:
What I find beautiful is that you have this mechanism for turning more computation into better intuition. Your policy network gives you an initial guess about which moves are promising. Then tree search spends more time thinking about those moves, exploring their consequences, and produces a better distribution over what to play. You train the policy network to predict that distribution.

So the thing that initially required all this search gradually becomes something the network can do in a single forward pass. And now, when you run search with that improved network, you can get an even better target. The policy improves the search, and the search improves the policy.

It’s a very elegant answer to the question of where the supervision comes from. You don’t need a human to tell you the best move at every position. You can use a slower, more computationally expensive version of your own decision process as a teacher, and then distill that back into your intuition.

r001.rationale: The response says tree search produces a better distribution over moves and that the policy network is trained to predict that distribution, distinguishing the target from a single selected move.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing the role of soft targets by retraining on the single actions selected by MCTS.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find beautiful is that the search gives you a way to turn more computation into a better training target. You start with a policy network that has some intuition about which moves are promising. Then you run Monte Carlo tree search, which uses that intuition but also explores the consequences of different moves. The distribution of visits at the root is, in a sense, a more considered version of the network’s initial guess.

And then you train the network to predict that distribution. So you’re taking something that required this expensive process of deliberation and distilling it into a single forward pass. What was previously search becomes intuition.

That creates this lovely feedback loop: better intuition makes search more effective, and better search produces better targets for intuition. You don’t need someone to tell you what the right move is at every position. You have a procedure for improving your own answers, and then learning to produce those improved answers more directly.

r001.rationale: The response says the root visit distribution is the training target and that the network is trained to predict that distribution, rather than a single selected move.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose testing soft targets by retraining on MCTS-selected actions instead.
